faq.q: When is the longest day of the year?
faq.a: In the northern hemisphere it is the June solstice, around 21 June. In the southern hemisphere the longest day comes around 21 December.
When your half of the Earth tilts towards the Sun, the Sun's daily path across the sky is longer and higher, so it rises earlier and sets later. More of each turn of the Earth is spent in sunlight.
asks: Why does it stay light so late in summer?

faq.q: Are day and night really equal at the equinox?
faq.a: Very nearly. They are about 12 hours each, though daytime is a few minutes longer, because sunrise is counted from when the Sun's top edge appears and the air bends sunlight over the horizon.

faq.q: Do places on the equator have long summer days?
faq.a: No. Near the equator, day and night stay close to 12 hours all year round. The difference grows the further you go towards the poles.
asks: Why don't days change length at the equator?

faq.q: How short is the shortest day?
faq.a: In London, the shortest day, around 21 December, has less than 8 hours of daylight. In the far north of Norway, the Sun doesn't rise at all for weeks.

facts: London gets about 16 hours 38 minutes of daylight at the June solstice and about 7 hours 50 minutes at the December solstice.
At the equator, the length of daylight stays close to 12 hours all year.

quiz.say: Where on Earth does the length of the day change the least through the year?
quiz.why: At the equator the Sun's daily path is split almost evenly between day and night all year, so days stay near 12 hours.

wrong.0: London's days range from under 8 hours to over 16 hours.
wrong.1: Near the pole the change is biggest, from no daylight to round-the-clock daylight.
